Boundaries: a 64 KiB instance id, one holding a NUL escape, and a non-ASCII one were each answered 200, none crashed the listener.

proof.criterion: A5/R6 under the concurrent run: a live holder that is heartbeating never loses its role to another client instance's claims and deregistrations.
proof.surface: The same real listener and nats-server over HTTP, with three actors firing at once in each round: the holder re-registering, a fresh foreign session soft-claiming the role and naming the holder as its predecessor, and that foreign instance deregistering the holder's session under its own id.
proof.command: cd -- "$LEGION_WORKSPACE" && bash /legion/scratch/tester/race.sh  (40 rounds, three concurrent actors each; a scratch rig, kept out of the tree)
proof.observed: rounds 40: refused=40 granted=0 roleMoved=0. The holder held the role at the end and its entry was still registered, so 40 concurrent foreign deregistrations removed nothing and 40 concurrent foreign claims took nothing. The whole run took 5.8s, so no round came near the route's 3.5s budget.
proof.negativeControl: The run counts the refusal it must see rather than only the absence of harm: a claim answered 200 would have been counted as granted and, had the role moved, the round would have printed 'THE ROLE MOVED'. granted=0 and roleMoved=0 together, against refused=40, is what distinguishes a rule that holds from a listener that answered nothing at all.

observations: A whitespace-only client_instance_id on DELETE /v1/sessions/<id> is trimmed to empty (api.go:638) and so takes the no-instance path (api.go:641), which deletes the entry unconditionally and answers 200 with no body. Measured: the entry was gone afterwards. This is R7's stated rule for a request naming no instance, and no client sends whitespace — both clients send newClientInstanceID()'s 128 random bits — so it is behaviour worth knowing rather than a defect.

The instance id is not readable through any read route: a session registered with the id SECRET-INSTANCE-ID is named by neither GET /v1/sessions nor GET /v1/registry/<id> (both answered 0 matches), because sessionInfo (api.go:787-804) carries no such field. The whole rule rests on one client being unable to name another's instance, so this is the property that makes it worth anything, and it holds.

A 64 KiB client_instance_id is accepted and stored (200). So are a 64 KiB title and a 64 KiB dir, measured side by side, so the new field adds no class of unbounded client-supplied string that the registry entry did not already carry; the route's 413 is for a NATS key or subject that is too long (api.go:200-217), not for field sizes.

Every registration and every deregistration in the two clients carries the id, and the module makes that structural rather than conventional: RegistrationInput is Omit<SubscribeInput, 'clientInstanceID'> (registration-state.ts:55), so no call site in pi-envoy can send a registration without it — the one subscribe is registration-state.ts:364 and the one unregister is :811. In claude-envoy all three sites pass it (envoy-channel-server.ts:765 registration, :938 the handoff deregistration, :1247 shutdown). createRegistrationState mints one id per call (registration-state.ts:291) and is called inside envoyExtension (envoy.ts:2034, inside the default export at :547), so two extension instances in one Oh My Pi process are two client instances, as the spec's design says.

bun.lock on this branch and on main@origin both record packages/pi-envoy 13.1.0 and packages/envoy-plugin 11.1.0, while their package.json files carry 13.10.0 and 12.5.0, so a plain `bun install` rewrites three lines of bun.lock. It is main's state, not this change's, and this pull request does not touch the file; I restored it after installing.
